How Product Cannibalization Fueled a $2 Billion Flywheel Volodymyr Khomichenko 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size A backyard sprinkler toy, a t-shirt strategy, and the month a startup discovered its ad spend was worthless. Here’s the story of Kajabi. Kajabi wasn’t supposed to be a software company. It was supposed to be a toy. In 2009, a software engineer named Kenny Rueter built a PVC pipe contraption in his Orange County backyard — basically a garden-hose-powered car wash for his kids’ bikes. The neighborhood kids loved it. Parents started asking where they could get one. Rueter and his friend Travis Rosser looked into manufacturing plastic pipes and shipping them to strangers. Then they looked at each other and said: absolutely not. Instead, they’d sell instructions. A digital course. Easy, right? Wrong. Building the actual website to sell that course became a nightmare of duct-taped tools — a merchant account here, a clunky WordPress plugin there, some sketchy video hosting, an email tool that didn’t talk to any of it. That frustration was the real business. Not the sprinkler. The platform that removed all that friction for anyone else with a “sprinkler idea” of their own. Fifteen years later, that platform is worth $2 billion — and the way it got there breaks most of the rules you’d expect a SaaS company to follow. Selling Prestige to an Ugly Industry Back then, the online education world was ruled by “info marketers” — the kind of people hawking $2,000 boxes of DVDs with sales pages that looked like ransom notes. Everything screamed “get rich quick.” Rueter and Rosser saw white space in the ugliness. What if someone built the Shopify of digital courses — something that actually looked legitimate? They weren’t trying to out-hustle the hustlers. They were trying to make the whole category feel less like a scam and more like a real business. The Growth Hack Before the Product Existed Here’s the part that should make every early-stage founder rethink their launch strategy. Kajabi didn’t cold-launch. They didn’t buy ads. They didn’t even have a public product yet. Instead, they quietly gave free access to the biggest names in internet marketing at the time — Frank Kern, Jeff Walker, Andy Jenkins — and let them run their huge, high-dollar course launches on it. Buried in the footer of every one of those pages: Powered by Kajabi. Click it, and you’d land on a page that said, essentially, “put your email here and we’ll tell you what this is later.” That’s it. That was the entire funnel. By the official launch on October 14, 2010, roughly 10,000 people were already on the waitlist — pre-sold, because they’d watched people they trusted succeed on this mystery platform. Kajabi crossed a million dollars in annual recurring revenue almost immediately, without spending a dollar on traditional advertising. The Decision That Should Have Killed the Company For five years, Kajabi ran quietly and profitably. The founders worked out of a small office in Old Town Tustin, coached their kids’ Little League teams, and turned down outside investors. Then, around 2015, the ground shifted. Teachable and Udemy showed up. The “all-in-one” platform that once felt revolutionary started to feel dated. Most founders in that position patch things up. Rueter did the opposite. He rebuilt the entire product from scratch — not to improve the existing tool, but to make it obsolete. He was willing to destroy his own revenue-generating product before a competitor got the chance to. The rebuild wasn’t just a facelift. It turned Kajabi from “a place to build one course” into a full business operating system — landing pages, email marketing, and CRM, all under one roof. To fund the transition, they offered early adopters a locked-in annual rate of $997, guaranteed never to increase. Three million dollars came in within two weeks. No venture capital required. The Month They Turned Off All Their Ads By 2016, Jonathan Cronstedt (“JCron”) joined as President, brought in to scale a $6 million business into something much bigger. Then came the experiment that changed everything. Kajabi was spending $1 million a month on paid ads, and the marketing team insisted the numbers were incredible. Cronstedt and Rueter didn’t fully buy it. So they shut off every paid campaign for thirty days. Growth didn’t move. At all. That’s when they realized the ad spend had never been the engine. The real growth driver was something much harder to fake: an organic flywheel built on product experience and community. So they stopped trying to buy customers and started celebrating the ones they had. Turning Customer Wins Into Free Advertising Running a business alone, staring at an empty dashboard, is isolating — and that isolation is exactly where most new users quit before making their first sale. Kajabi’s answer became one of the smartest retention plays in SaaS: the Kajabi Hero program. Hit your first $1,000 in sales? A physical t-shirt shows up at your door. Sounds small. It wasn’t. That shirt became a badge — something people photographed and posted proudly in the private community. Each post was free social proof, reinforcing the same “Powered by Kajabi” loop that built the company in the first place. Eventually the tiers escalated to $100,00
